title: Tesla launches flying Roadster concept car
description: Electric car company Tesla has unveiled its flying Roadster vehicle with a demonstration in which the car drove upside down, flipped off a ramp and briefly flew, using compressed-air thrusters that Tesla claims will make it the world's quickest production car. During a live event in Texas, the two-seat Roadster model drove up a half-pipe ramp and launched off the top, remaining in the air for a few seconds before landing It also became airborne after building up speed on flat ground, launching over a row of parked vehicles. It then lifted off from a stationary position. Tesla has unveiled its second-generation Roadster A series of thrusters in the bottom and back propelled the car into the air and cushioned the landings. It was designed by Tesla and SpaceX, both companies led by businessman Elon Musk, who called the second-generation Roadster "a collaboration with the world's best car company and the world's best rocket company". It has thrusters that use compressed air The thrusters can also fire rearward to boost acceleration. Tesla demonstrated the car reaching 60 miles per hour in a claimed 0.81 seconds, and said it would be the "quickest" production vehicle to 60 miles per hour. On the half-pipe ramp, the vehicle was able to remain upside down due to a fan suction system. The air tanks in the vehicle are rechargeable and can be recompressed without fuel, according to Tesla. The vehicle uses compressed air to take off and land Long term, Musk said the car will be the "only manual" vehicle in its lineup, referencing plans for driverless vehicles . Though the demonstration used a pre-programmed sequence with no driver. Tesla chief designer Franz von Holzhausen said the car was designed with an "aerospace aesthetic". It has an angular supercar exterior with scissor doors and a deployable spoiler, and is a coupe with a hard top. Read: Videos reveal vertical takeoff of electric flying car in California The seats are moulded directly to the chassis, and it features wire steering, which replaces the mechanical link between the steering wheel and wheels with electronic controls. Musk referenced the uncertainty of street legality for the flying capabilities and said that " success is not guaranteed" before the test. The company gave it an "aerospace aesthetic" Production on the vehicle is set for 2028, according to Tesla. The company first unveiled a second-generation Roadster in 2017 , with deliveries planned for 2020. Tesla's last major launch was the Cybertruck , unveiled in 2019. Other recent concept cars include Alef's concept vehicle . The imagery is courtesy of Tesla. The post Tesla launches flying Roadster concept car appeared first on Dezeen .

Check it out ! “ coincidence ,” by K Bahr on Flickr “A coincidence, after all, has to be noticed.“ Dear friend of TAoN Suzanne M sent me a link the other day to a deep-dive article about coincidences . I’d never given this subject much thought, but it turned out to be pretty interesting. And as Suzanne detected, there was a noticing/attention angle that I couldn’t help dwelling on. A coincidence, after all, has to be noticed. If I walk past a childhood friend I haven’t seen in 20 years in some airport where neither of us lives, one of us has to notice the other for the coincidence to “count,” as it were. In some ways, “ the amazing thing is not that these things occur, it’s that we notice them, ” according to David Spiegelhalter, a professor at the University of Cambridge who studies such things, as quoted in Julie Beck’s’ Atlantic article. You could say that being more attentive leads to registering more coincidences. Spiegelhalter, the article notes, has a website where people can submit their coincidence experiences, and claims to have collected something like 5,000 of them. The most common form is “ finding a link with someone you meet .” Obviously, this suggests that people who are looking for connections — who are open, curious, attentive to others — are more likely to find unexpected ones. “Coincidences never happen to me at all, because I never notice anything,” Spiegelhalter says (somewhat jokingly). “I never talk to anybody on trains. If I’m with a stranger, I don’t try to find a connection with them … .” I admit it never really occurred to me that there could be coincidence-friendly types . But Beck also cites another researcher who has found that certain personality traits are linked to experiencing more coincidences—people who describe themselves as religious or spiritual, people who are self-referential (or likely to relate information from the external world back to themselves), and people who are high in meaning-seeking are all coincidence-prone. The article goes on to explore everything from Jung’s idea of synchronicity to popular notions of the paranormal. Possibly the opposite of missing coincidences is reading too much meaning into mere chance occurrences that look like something more. The world shapes our attention, but sometimes attention shapes our world — for better or worse! That said, I’m attracted to this idea that “finding a link with someone you meet” is the most-reported form of coincidence. It’s a nice frame for chatting with someone new: Be curious, be open — and look for a happy coincidence or two. Leave a comment Thank you Suzanne! Noticing is about other people, too. title: #305 | Offline é o novo hype (parte 2)
description: nas edições anteriores #303 | Marcas multiespécie #304 | Offline é o novo hype (parte 1) tempo de leitura: 4 minutos para entender 💡 Passamos os últimos dois anos falando, desejando, criando, repetindo o termo “offline” nos nossos planos de mídia e carrosseis de Instagram, a ponto dele ter se tornado também um grande hype . Por um lado, pessoas performando atividades online apenas para postar. Por outro, marcas usando esse movimento como desculpa pra poluir visualmente o mundo real ou encher as nossas casas de objetos desnecessários. (Nem tudo deveria ter um anúncio. O mundo não precisa de mais um brinde com o seu logo sem intenção nenhuma). E agora? _ Este não é um manifesto anti-offline. De maneira alguma. A gente não deve desistir de materializar as nossas marcas ou criar experiências no mundo real (não vamos desistir) . Mas neste processo, é importante entender duas coisas: 1. “Offline é o novo luxo” é uma maneira muito simplista de olhar para essa tendência. Ela é indiscutivelmente atrativa para as marcas de luxo, que sempre pautaram a sua comunicação na estética e estilos de vida capazes de diferenciar as pessoas. Quando a estética “comum” é cronicamente online, feita por IA e vidrada em uma tela, o luxo busca ilustrações feitas à mão e experiências sensoriais. Mas a necessidade de desconectar vai além da performance e da distinção social. O que torna o “offline” um movimento muito maior que qualquer trend é justamente a sua capacidade de resgatar uma série de aspectos que têm se perdido na vida moderna. A presença, a atenção, o processo, o aprendizado, a conexão com outras pessoas, a dificuldade (e, consequentemente, a resiliência)… E as tantas sensações, rituais e habilidades que só o mundo real proporciona. Objetos físicos, eventos e atividades manuais devem seguir parte da estratégia das marcas. Não para gerar percepção de luxo ou para fazer igual a uma ou outra. Muito menos para criar novos espaços de mídia que “chamam mais atenção”. E sim pela sua capacidade de interromper o scroll infinito, de ser um lembrete da vida que acontece fora das telas, de gerar valor e, quem sabe, até transformação real nas pessoas. O que nos leva ao segundo ponto. _ 2. Quando o offline se torna hype, é preciso fugir do lugar comum Em 2025, fizemos a primeira edição de uma revista impressa. Ela foi a realização de um sonho antigo, e a materialização da Bits to Brands em cores, ilustrações e páginas enviadas para todo o Brasil. Seu projeto editorial foi feito em outubro de 2024, e a sua impressão em dezembro. Na época, as revistas já começavam a despontar como símbolo de nostalgia - mas não dava para imaginar que seria um movimento tão intenso. Desde então, diversas marcas imprimiram revistas - e serviram café, receberam clubes do livro, ofereceram corridas de rua, distribuíram bonés bordados, estamparam câmeras analógicas… Assim, apenas na sua segunda edição, uma revista não é mais surpreendente ou inovadora. Do mesmo jeito que, em 2026, um boné também não é. (Aliás, um boné vira parte de uma coleção que está chegando a 20 unidades por aqui) O valor do offline não vai a lugar nenhum, mas fazer o básico não é mais o suficiente. O desafio é seguir se reinventando no mesmo formato. A boa notícia é que aí mora a diversão. Porque na tentativa de despertar o que há de mais humano em alguém (a presença, o contato, a memória), precisamos ser humanos primeiro . (criativos, sensíveis, curiosos). Fazer mais ou menos do mesmo jeito, mas um pouco diferente. Fazer mais ou menos a mesma coisa, mas fazer também algo novo. Tornar algo uma tradição, investir de fato em um ritual de marca - mas buscar novas formas de encontrar prazer no processo, e encantar as pessoas com o resultado. Uma revista, a gente já tinha feito. title: #304 | Offline é o novo hype (parte 1)
description: nas edições anteriores #302 | Os oráculos da timeline #303 | Marcas multiespécie tempo de leitura: 5 minutos para entender 💡 Já vai fazer dois anos que a expressão “o offline é o novo luxo” se disseminou pela internet. Ora como análise de tendência, ora como sinalização de virtude. Nós também somos um pouco culpados disso: Em janeiro de 2025, prestes a lançar a primeira edição da nossa revista impressa, estávamos mergulhados no “offline”. E não só a gente. Foi um verão em que muita gente procurou desconectar, e assim seguiu pelas estações. De câmeras analógicas a aulas de cerâmica, palavras cruzadas, telefones fixos… Todo tipo de estratégia (e produto) foi surgindo para ajudar. Começando, inclusive, pelas marcas de luxo. Porque não é uma coincidência que este seja o adjetivo mais utilizado ao lado da palavra “offline”. Tanto porque o “luxo” é mais valioso e raro, quanto porque ele é aquilo que foge do comum. Quando uma estética ou comportamento se torna o básico, aquilo que todo mundo tem, beirando até o “brega” - performar superioridade intelectual e social é se afastar dela. (A relação entre consumo e performance social está super bem explicada em Coisa de Rico , de Michel Alcoforado). Se nos últimos anos o comum é ser hiperconectado, cronicamente online e passar incontáveis horas arrastando para cima imóvel, o que passa a comunicar luxo e status é desconectar. Ler livros de verdade, fazer atividade física ao ar livre, acessórios tecnológicos mais vintage, encontros para discutir temas específicos, o resgate dos hábitos e atividades sociais das avós (do tricô ao nonna-maxxing )… É por essas e outras que a Miu Miu tem um clube do livro, a Bottega Veneta lançou um jogo de Jenga, a Prada fez uma floricultura e as marcas de luxo têm disputado espaço para fazer ativações nos grandes torneios de tênis pelo mundo. O offline se tornou, sim, sinônimo de luxo. Mas não pára por aí. _ O offline se tornou território de desejo das marcas por motivos certos e errados, racionais e abstratos, mas muitos deles ancorados em comportamentos e demandas bem reais. Um deles é a distinção social. Mas ativações no mundo real, eventos, experiências e objetos físicos despertam interesse também porque são comunitários, sensoriais, duráveis, memoráveis e humanos. Cada um desses aspectos parte de demandas da vida contemporânea que começam no excesso de telas, mas se estendem para a ausência de interações sociais, a substituição do corpo físico pela imagem editada de alguém e até o tal “AI Slop”. Num parque a gente não precisa ficar se perguntando se algo é IA ou não a cada dois minutos (ainda). Porque o offline é comunidade , ele nos permite lembrar que não estamos sozinhos nos nossos gostos e hobbies - seja correr uma meia maratona, seja ter sido fã da Xuxa na infância. Porque o offline é sensorial , ele nos lembra que cada um é um corpo, e não apenas um cérebro e as pontas dos dedos. E que um corpo é capaz de sentir gostos, cheiros, toques, de dançar, cantar, esbarrar, ver e ser visto e se relacionar - de verdade. Porque o offline é durável , ele se torna representação no mundo real de quem a gente é. Aquilo que decora os nossos ambientes, que compõe as nossas coleções , que está pendurado nas nossas bolsas e mochilas ou até geladeiras - ajuda a contar a nossa história. Diga-me o que colecionas e te direi quem és. Porque o offline é memorável, ele é uma grande oportunidade para as marcas investirem seus orçamentos de comunicação de forma mais assertiva. Estamos descobrindo que reunir um grupo de pessoas verdadeiramente atentas e interessadas tem mais valor do que atingir milhões de views sabe-se lá de quem. E porque o offline é humano, ele é o único ambiente onde a gente vivencia o tempo de forma linear, a arte de forma artesanal e o mundo conforme a nossa própria curadoria de experiências - e não a de um algortimo. Não é à toa que todo mundo quer mais disso. _ Passamos os últimos dois anos falando, desejando, criando, repetindo o termo “offline” nos nossos planos de mídia e carrosseis de Instagram, a ponto dele ter se tornado também um grande hype . Por um lado, pessoas performando atividades online apenas para postar. Por outro, marcas usando esse movimento como desculpa pra poluir visualmente o mundo real ou encher as nossas casas de objetos desnecessários. (Nem tudo deveria ter um anúncio. O mundo não precisa de mais um brinde com o seu logo sem intenção nenhuma). E agora? _ continua na próxima edição. para continuar a conversa nas redes sociais e convidar mais gente para cá, compartilhe usando o botão abaixo ou marcando a @bitstobrands Share para inspirar ✨ Ao invés de só um case, vocês aceitam três? :) Como parte da nossa estratégia de ser verdadeiramente multicanal (com conteúdo feito para cada plataforma) e inspirar as pessoas por trás das marcas brasileiras e no Brasil, surgiu a #BrasilnaBits. E se você tiver sugestões, pode deixar aqui nos comentários. para fazer parte da conversa 💬 O Instagram atualizou a sua tipografia e todo o seu universo visual . description: nas edições anteriores #298 | Cadê a conversão? #299 | Nesta Copa do Mundo, olhe em volta tempo de leitura: 4 minutos para entender 💡 “No jantar, um cirurgião me perguntou por que eu escrevo com uma caneta, ao invés de usar um ditafone ou processador de palavras. - Por que eu faria isso? - Porque é mais rápido e mais eficiente - Mas este é o trabalho da minha vida. Eu não tenho pressa”. Helen Garner, em 1984. _ “A Bits precisa ganhar vida…” foi uma frase muito repetida por aqui nos últimos meses. E, se vamos ser bem honestos, ela seguia com “...para além de mim” . Nas muitas folhas de papel em que cenários foram desenhados, era como se até aqui a Bits precisasse da Beatriz para existir - e era chegado o momento da sua independência. Pensem numa dor de crescimento. Maravilhosa, pois em oito anos a gente cresceu muito . Mas não menos doída. A Bits to Brands se tornou uma empresa antes que “empreender” se tornasse uma habilidade por aqui. Uma conversa que a creator economy adora evitar, essa de que viver de conteúdo é mais estruturar processos e fluxos de caixa do que ter ideias brilhantes que podem viralizar. Mais economy , menos creator . Enquanto tenta vender produtos que mudam o tempo inteiro, para clientes que pagam em 90 dias, com um big boss que oscila as suas métricas sem nenhuma lógica aparente. Coisa de gente meio maluca. Mas um dia você cria algo despretensiosamente, e aos poucos aquilo vai ganhando vida até que a sua existência se torna inegociável. Aí você negocia a sua rotina como CLT, o seu planejamento financeiro, as suas habilidades, o que significa “horário comercial”. Negocia os seus valores, seus limites, suas parcerias. E segue. _ 300 edições depois, há todo um planejamento estratégico baseado na capacidade de enxergar a Bits to Brands não mais como quem olha no espelho, mas como quem encara o horizonte. Porque a Bits é o trabalho da minha vida, mas eu sou apenas uma parte da vida dela. Nos grandes marcos até aqui, as reflexões sempre foram sobre o processo de criar, de começar, de continuar. Hoje, eu escolho celebrar o infinito do que vai além. Certamente muita coisa começa no som do teclado em uma noite silenciosa, ou num áudio animado com uma ideia que parece absurda. Só que incrível mesmo é o que acontece depois. Anos atrás, um garoto no interior do Mato Grosso leu centenas de edições do arquivo de uma newsletter e aquilo foi essencial pra que ele decidisse seguir carreira em comunicação. Hoje, ele trabalha na WPP. Há pouco mais de uma semana, uma mulher foi oficialmente contratada como professora de pós-graduação por causa de uma conversa que começou em um grupo de Whatsapp chamado “Comunidade Bits” . Tem também a dona de um café em Joinville que, na época do lançamento de Barbie, viu um post no Instagram da Bits sobre o hype de produtos com a cara do filme. Pois ela fez um bolinho rosa temático - e esgotou todas as unidades. Outro dia, chegando num grande evento para palestrar, uma moça se levantou da primeira fila e tirou da bolsa uma revista da Bits, que ela ganhou porque indicou a sua newsletter favorita para dezenas de pessoas, e guarda até hoje como algo especial. _ O “agora” exerce uma pressão imensa sobre a gente, o tempo todo. O formato em alta, o calendário de posts da semana, o assunto mais comentado do momento, a mais nova ferramenta de IA que vai fazer tudo por você. E a roda não para nunca de girar - há 300 edições e contando. Mas não dá para perder de vista tudo que acontece quando a gente cria algo, e aquilo que a gente cria ganha vida na vida de alguém. De maneira totalmente imprevisível, incontrolável e muitas vezes até irreversível. Como são todas as coisas grandiosas, e todas as coisas pequenas também. Uma de cada vez, elas se tornam o trabalho de uma vida. Em conjunto, elas ganham vida própria. Longa vida à Bits to Brands, e a tudo que existe no mundo porque ela existe. Todos os projetos, todos os clientes, todas as pessoas, todas as histórias, todas as ideias, todas as páginas (impressas e digitais) e toda inspiração que circula por todo o Brasil. title: Default Bias: Who chose your settings?
description: When a choice arrives with one option already set, most people leave it in place, regardless of whether it reflects their actual preference. The friction of changing something, combined with the implicit signal that the pre-set option is normal or recommended, produces consistent gravity toward the status quo. The mechanism runs through several channels at once. Loss aversion makes changing a default feel like risking something already owned. Implied endorsement suggests the default is a reasonable choice, so selecting it requires less justification. And the cognitive cost of evaluating alternatives encourages people to accept the existing state. These forces compound, especially in low-stakes or unfamiliar decisions where people lack strong preferences to override them. Default bias appears across organ donation programs, retirement savings enrollment, privacy settings, and software configuration. In each case, the same population of people produces dramatically different outcomes depending on which option requires action and which requires inaction. The default does not just simplify the interface. It determines the outcome for a large share of users. In design A user opens a new account and immediately lands in a signup flow. Before they have formed any preferences, the product has already decided: marketing emails are on, data sharing is enabled, notifications fire at full volume. The user clicks through, and the defaults stay. Default bias means the designer’s pre-set choices become most users’ permanent choices, whether or not those choices were made with the user’s benefit in mind. This places significant weight on the moment a default is chosen. Every pre-selected option is effectively a policy decision applied to the full user base. Designers who understand this use defaults to serve the majority, while keeping alternatives reachable. Those who ignore it discover that their defaults reflect internal convenience or business incentives rather than user needs. Applications in digital products Set the default communication preference to the least intrusive option, then let users escalate: email digests before individual notifications, not the reverse. When offering a free-to-paid upgrade, pre-select the plan that fits the user’s current usage, not the highest-tier plan, so the default reflects their situation. Place the destructive or irreversible action as the non-default: require an affirmative click to delete, unsubscribe, or share data, rather than treating those as pre-selected states. In onboarding forms, default empty fields to blank rather than placeholder values that users might submit without reading. On privacy and data settings, default to the most private configuration and present expansion as a deliberate user choice, not a correction of a setting they already “agreed to.” When a setting has a best-fit value for most users, pre-select it with a visible label like “Recommended” so the default carries transparent reasoning rather than hidden authority. Industry examples Countries with automatic organ donation enrollment see consent rates above 90%. Countries that require a positive registration act see rates below 20%. Same populations, different defaults. Thaler and Benartzi documented a similar pattern in 401(k) enrollment in 2003. Companies that switched retirement plans to automatic enrollment saw participation jump from around 50% to over 90%. Employees could still remove themselves. Most did not. Microsoft pre-selected telemetry and automatic update settings in Windows 10 that collected substantial user data. Changing them required navigating several menus. Few users did. Google enabled AI-assisted email completion in Gmail by default for all users. Adoption was high not because users chose it, but because disabling it required a deliberate action most skipped. Apple’s App Tracking Transparency, released in 2021, shifted ad tracking from an on-by-default state to an explicit prompt. Consent rates dropped from an estimated 70% to under 30%. No one changes what they don’t notice Changing a default requires two things most people avoid at the same time: forming a preference and acting on it. The pre-set option eliminates both requirements. People accept it without deliberating, often without noticing the choice was made. This is not a failure of attention, rather a rational response to cognitive load . When a decision is low-salience and the default seems reasonable, the cost of evaluating alternatives outweighs the benefit. The designer who sets the default has, in effect, already made the decision for the majority. This is why defaults carry ethical weight. A designer can claim to offer choice while structuring the choice so that most users never exercise it. Defaults are most powerful in one-time setup flows, where users move quickly and rarely return to revisit. Designers who want users to engage with settings should surface them at the moment of relevance, not bury them in preferences menus users open once and forget. Choosing the default is unavoidable. There is no neutral pre-selection. Every product that ships with a setting in place has already made a choice about whose interests that setting serves. Further reading The Power of Defaults — Jakob Nielsen, Nielsen Norman Group (2005) Defaults — The Decision Lab Status Quo Bias — The Decision Lab Choice Architecture 2.0: How People Interpret and Make Sense of Nudges — Job Krijnen, Behavioral Scientist (2018) Defaults Are Not the Same by Default — Jachimowicz, Duncan, Weber, and Johnson, Behavioral Scientist (2019) You just read why the pre-set option wins. So here’s one I’ve set for you: The reference designers keep open. Default Bias is 1 of 106 principles in Psychology of Design; the complete reference behind this newsletter. What attention does. How trust forms. Why habits stick. Each one written the way you just read this one: the mechanism, where it shows up, and how to use it. title: Spaces by Manah signposts Chennai community centre with barrel-vaulted roof
description: Local architecture studio Spaces by Manah has completed The Soil & Sea community centre in Chennai, India , with a brick barrel-vaulted roof that serves as a "visible landmark" on the site. The 4,330-square-metre building was designed to provide learning space for a local education centre, as well as to house community workshops and events. Spaces by Manah designed its single-storey masonry structure to appear as though it were "growing out of the existing landscape", creating a series of outdoor and open-air spaces that overlook its lush surroundings. Spaces by Manah has completed a community centre in Chennai, India "The project sits within a lush, tree-lined parcel of land with the design growing out of the existing landscape," the studio told Dezeen. "The building is positioned to retain its connection with the trees and outdoor spaces through a sequence of shaded, open and enclosed spaces, while the dominant barrel vault rises above the canopy to create a visible landmark within the site," it added. Raised on a rubble stone foundation, the centre is organised around a flat-roofed volume, flanked on two sides by an L-shaped verandah that was conceived by the studio as an "intermediate, informal zone" between the building and landscape. A barrel-vaulted roof crowns the gathering space Steps and a ramp at the building's front lead up to the verandah, which is sheltered by the barrel-vaulted roof on one side to form a main gathering space for the community. Meanwhile, its other edge is topped with a sloping, tiled roof. A series of granite stone pillars frame the space, along with built-in seating. Read: Sculptural music centre shows bamboo as "a serious construction material" "The architecture responds to this idea through a strong central gathering space, expressed by the barrel vault, with more intimate and informal spaces arranged around it," the studio said. "An L-shaped veranda acts as an intermediate, informal zone between the enclosed spaces and the landscape, with built-in seating and ramps supporting movement, accessibility and interaction throughout the building." Granite stone pillars and Mangalore tiles complement the building's brick walls The bricks used for the structure's load-bearing walls were left exposed throughout the space. To complement the brick design, the studio sourced doors, windows and Mangalore floor tiles locally and repurposed them throughout the building. This materiality extends to the building's interior, where exposed brick walls and roof elements are set off by glossy tiles. "The material palette was intentionally kept natural, tactile and largely raw, allowing the building to sit comfortably within its landscape," the studio said. Glossy tiles are used within the interior Also on the site is a separate toilet block, which is similarly perched atop a stone foundation, and complete with load-bearing brick walls and a tiled canopy roof. Elsewhere in Chennai, Ekarth Studio has used bamboo to form a sculptural venue for the Maestro Ilaiyaraaja Centre for Music Learning and Research , while Habitat Collaborative has threaded a curved school through a tree-filled site in Vadodara . title: Factory in Bangladesh that "redefines manufacturing architecture" wins RIBA International Prize
description: A rug factory in Rangpur, Bangladesh , designed by Dhaka-based studio Nakshabid Architects to dismantle workplace hierarchies, has won the RIBA International Prize for 2026. Named Green Field Factory, the project is the fifth winner of the biennial award, presented by the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) to the world's best new building outside the UK. Nakshabid Architects was praised by the RIBA jury for designing a factory that incorporates passive design principles and prioritises the wellbeing of its 5,000 employees. Green Field Factory won this year's RIBA International Prize. Photo by City Syntax "Green Field Factory redefines manufacturing architecture in South Asia and beyond," said RIBA president Christ Williamson. "By putting people, wellbeing and their everyday experiences at its core and actively supporting its female workforce, it proves that thoughtful design can dismantle traditional hierarchies to create profound social and environmental change." It was announced as the RIBA International Prize winner at the Stirling Prize ceremony in London last night. This year's prestigious Stirling Prize was given to Mary Duggan Architects and Ruff Architects for the Lion Green Road housing development in London. The factory has a monumental green wall. Photo by City Syntax Commissioned by rug manufacturer Karupannya Rangpur Limited , Green Field Factory is a seven-storey building surrounded by fields and small settlements. Nakshabid Architects based the design on the traditional Bengali home, incorporating natural ventilation and biophilic design principles. Courtyards, verandas, gardens and a monumental green facade were designed to let natural light and airflow into the building, minimising the need for mechanical systems. Nakshabid Architects designed the building with passive ventilation. Photo by Prantography Green Field Factory has one main entrance with two grand staircases for all workers, intended to challenge hierarchies in the workplace. This responds to other factories in the area that have separate entrances for factory workers and people in management roles. Shared spaces in the factory provide areas for workers to take breaks and socialise. Other areas are designated to support workers' families and the wider community during the day and outside of working hours, including a rooftop daycare centre, on-site medical practice, grocery shop and prayer room. A connection to nature is provided through low-maintenance planting throughout, which also supports insects and birds, while artwork and sculptures celebrate the role of women in the workplace, family and community. Read: "Welcoming and inclusive" London housing wins RIBA Stirling Prize 2026 "The project demonstrates the dissolution of architecture as a topological space, with a single-pointed focus on dismantling civilisational oppression and hierarchy, for woman and man alike," said grand jury chair Bijoy Jain. "Through the simple gesture of two grand stairs as an equanimous shared portal, it transforms a space and symbol once reserved exclusively for the king of the region, as landlord and ruling class, and for the colonial power that pervaded the length and breadth of the country," he continued. "The architect and owner shared how the women and men working in the factory would bring their families with pride to show them where they worked, and the women empowered in their self-reliance to take life and familial decisions on their own." The jury praised the design for prioritising the wellbeing of the factory employees. Photo by Karupannya Rangpur The RIBA International Prize is awarded biennially to a building that "demonstrates visionary, innovative thinking, and design excellence whilst making a distinct contribution for its users and within its physical context". Green Field Factory was selected ahead of BRAC University in Bangladesh by WOHA, Z33 art museum in Belgium by Francesca Torzo Architetto and the renovation of Royale Belge in Belgium by Caruso St John Architects, Bovenbouw Architectuur and DDS+. YIMBY by Maker Architecten was named the winner of the International Emerging Architect Award. Photo by Stijn Bollaert Alongside the International Prize, RIBA awarded this year's International Emerging Architect Award to Maker Architecten for its YIMBY residential project in Kortrijk, Belgium. The project revamped 18 plots across a 1920's garden city neighbourhood, utilising reclaimed materials for new facades and creating communal green space. In 2024, Peris + Toral Arquitectes won the RIBA International Prize for an "inclusive and sustainable" social housing project in Barcelona. The top photo is by Mud Canvas. title: "Welcoming and inclusive" London housing wins RIBA Stirling Prize 2026
description: The Lion Green Road housing in south London, designed by local studios Mary Duggan Architects with Ruff Architects, has won this year's RIBA Stirling Prize for the UK's best new building. Located in Coulsdon, the high-density development commissioned by Croydon Council provides 157 homes across five blocks, which are stitched together by a series of shared green spaces. Lion Green Road has won the RIBA Stirling Prize 2026 The Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) named the project as winner of the prestigious prize at a ceremony in London this evening. It is the fourth housing scheme to win the prize since its inception 30 years ago, following Accordia in Cambridge in 2008, Goldsmith Street in Norwich in 2019 and Appleby Blue Almshouse in London in 2025. The development comprises five blocks staggered across a sloped site. Photo by RIBA The jury hailed Mary Duggan Architects and Ruff Architects for "addressing the pressing need for national housing" and providing environmentally considerate homes with ample access to light, nature and community. "More than a housing development, the scheme has created a welcoming and inclusive place where people can connect with one another, and with nature," read the citation. Lion Green Road comprises five blocks with a mix of private and socially rented homes. They are staggered across its steeply sloped site – a topographically challenging plot previously used as a car park. The blocks have faceted, star-shaped plans, which are rotated to offer unique views across the landscape and ensure each home is dual-aspect, maximising natural light. The blocks are unified by three different brick types A trio of complementary brick types clad the buildings, helping to visually unify them while giving each its own unique aesthetic. Shared outdoor spaces that weave through the blocks enhance this unification, giving residents opportunities to meet and engage with each other. RIBA said the project addresses "the pressing need for national housing" RIBA president Chris Williamson said the scheme demonstrates how high-density housing "can be achieved without compromising the quality of the places we create". "Through a consistent specification, with subtle variation in height and orientation, it offers housing at scale without uniformity," he reflected. "The architects have created a new kind of garden neighbourhood that balances privacy and generous views with a strong connection to nature – it's a living landscape," Williamson continued. "This is thoughtful, resourceful architecture that proves that even the most challenging of sites can be transformed into truly distinctive places for people to call home." Read: "Hopeful and imaginative" social housing wins RIBA Stirling Prize 2025 The RIBA Stirling Prize has been awarded annually to the UK's best new building since 1996. Lion Green Road was chosen from a six-strong shortlist, revealed in July . It was announced as this year's winner at a ceremony at Old Billingsgate this evening, where RIBA also revealed the recipients of its five Special Awards. This included the RIBA Neave Brown Award for Housing, which was won by Satish Jassal Architects for Rowan Court , a cluster of brick-clad social housing blocks in Seven Sisters. Collaborators Samuel Chisholm Studio and Takero Shimazaki took home the RIBA Reinvention Award for Oru Sutton, a co-working space in an old department store, while Tonkin Liu Architects won the RIBA Client of the Year Award in recognition of the York Minster Centre of Excellence. Finally, the RIBA Conservation Award was given to Architectural Thread for The Buttermarket, an arts-focused community hub in Cornwall, which also won the RIBA Stephen Lawrence Prize for emerging architectural talent. Green spaces are woven through the site. Photo by RIBA Previous winners of the Stirling Prize include London's Elizabeth Line in 2024, The New Library at Magdalene College in 2022 and a seaside pier in Hastings in 2017. Last year's award, which was won by the "hopeful and imaginative" Appleby Blue Almshouse social housing , sparked concerns about London bias , with four of the six shortlisted buildings located in the capital city. Earlier this year, the shortlist for the 2026 Stirling Prize was a topic of conversation in our Dezeen Weekly podcast, with our journalists pondering if architecture has become too boring . title: "Radically simple" Resonance pavilion takes centre stage at Tallinn Architecture Biennale
description: Limestone and plywood make up the temporary pavilion at the heart of this year's Tallinn Architecture Biennale , designed by Shanghai- and Tokyo-based studio Aru Ma- Architects. Named Resonance, the pavilion was the winning entry of a competition hosted by the 2026 Tallinn Architecture Biennale (TAB) for its central pavilion, which sits outside the Estonian Museum of Architecture. The Resonance pavilion forms the heart of Tallinn Architecture Biennale Resonance was designed from a palette of what Aru Ma- Architects called "ordinary materials" and is intended as a comment on how luxury can be achieved with limited resources. It responds to this year's curatorial theme at the TAB, How Much?, which invites discourse about the role of money in architecture. This is also the focus of the festival's main exhibition, developed by this year's curator, Estonian architecture practice Stuudio Täna . It sits outside the Estonian Museum of Architecture "The pavilion uses standard construction materials in unexpected ways, elevating them into something new and unique," said Stuudio Täna architect Kertu Johanna Jõeste. "A spatially intriguing visual is accomplished with radically simple techniques and materials, aligning the pavilion very well with the topics of TAB 2026." Read: Reclaimed materials shape Copenhagen Architecture Biennial pavilion by Slaatto Morsbøl The pavilion takes the form of a square inward-facing courtyard, intended to offer respite from its busy surroundings on a traffic island. It is built from a palette of rebar, rope, limestone and plywood, offering a deliberately pared-back, timeless aesthetic, while ensuring the structure can be easily demounted at the end of the festival. Limestone ballasts the structure According to Aru Ma- Architects, its structure is "a carefully balanced tensile structure", with a limestone core as a ballast. "The project transforms strict economic and material constraints into an immersive architectural environment shaped by light, wind, sound, and gravity," the studio said. It has a deliberately pared-back material palette TAB is an international architecture and urban planning festival, which has taken place in the Estonian capital every two years since 2011. This year's edition takes place from 9 September to 30 November 2026. Previous central pavilions at the event include the Fungible Non-Fungible Pavilion , which had a puzzle-like structure partly designed by the public, and a bus shelter built from reclaimed materials . The photography is by Martin Siplane. The 2026 edition of Tallinn Architecture Biennale runs from 9 September to 30 November. title: Wild, As In Harmonious
description: * Reminder: The Savor of the Month theme for September is STRIPES. Details here ; Supporters can share their findings in the thread here . So many great contributions! Check it out ! “You need to go out into the world and look.” If you pay attention to the idea of paying attention, you have no doubt encountered the words of Mary Oliver, from her poems, essays, interviews. Oliver attracted fans ranging from John Waters to Oprah, from Stephen Colbert to Lucy Dacus. In The Art of Noticing book, I quoted from her poem “ Sometimes ”: Instructions for living a life: Pay attention. Be astonished. Tell about it. But the truth is, I didn’t really know much about Oliver’s life, and even my familiarity with her work was pretty thin. So I was very excited to see the new documentary about her, Mary Oliver: Saved By the Beauty of the World, via the PBS series American Masters. You can watch on the PBS site , or on YouTube . I recommend it! The documentary covers Oliver’s career as well her personal life, traumas included. (The title borrows from her line: “I got saved by poetry, and I got saved by the beauty of the world.”) I won’t attempt to summarize the whole thing, but I’ll share some of of the TAoN- relevant highlights. Oliver grew up in Ohio, an outsider drawn mostly to the natural world and “dead poets.” She preferred noticing to being noticed. Later, in her 20s, she learned from the intensity with which her partner, photographer Molly Malone Cook, interacted with others. Another of her familiar quotations: “ Attention without feeling … is only a report. ” Oliver and Cook lived in Provincetown, where Oliver continued her practice, attentive and poetic, walking the same paths to discover what she missed before. In time, she won major awards, and a significant audience, but to some extent the literary establishment pigeonholed her as someone who basically just went for walks and wrote about it. One person in the documentary calls her an icon of the hermit life. But that’s not the whole story. “You need to go out into the world and look,” the poet Mark Doty says in the documentary, and that’s exactly what Oliver was doing — even if it was in the nearby woods. Her appreciation of the natural world was no retreat. It was the opposite. “ Attention is the beginning of devotion, ” as she (famously) wrote in the title essay of her collection Upstream . This is perhaps her central lesson for those of us who care to go out into the world land look. “You can get ecstatic over a box of matches,” she remarks in one interview clip. And in other she makes the point I love the most: “If you love something, you give it a lot of attention. And if you give something a lot of attention, you very often learn to love it.” Yet another widely quoted Oliver line is her poetic question : “ what is it you plan to do with your one wild and precious life? ” Her own life might not sound “wild” in the way we commonly use that word. But if you don’t have time for the whole documentary, check out the clip below discussing her poem “ Wild Geese ” — and ultimately pointing out that wild can also mean natural, harmonious. If I were in New York I would go to THWACK: An Ode To Production , from Mmuseumm — even though I have no idea what it is. (“Sept. 9 ranks 1st out of 366 days, with an average of 12,344 births per day.”) The Restroom Archive “features 3D scans of nearly 100 [public] lavatories from around the world,” reports Popular Science . In other bathroom news, Design Week has a bit of a dive on restrooms as a design opportunity for the hospitality business. “The journey to the loo can be one of the most powerful storytelling opportunities in a venue.” Hm. description: nas edições anteriores #299 | Nesta Copa do Mundo, olhe em volta #300 | A vida das coisas tempo de leitura: 5 minutos para entender 💡 Às vésperas da Copa do Mundo, em 2022, comentamos na edição 188 que era a primeira Copa pós-TikTok e a primeira Copa pós-Casimiro. O que mudou o jeito de transmitir, de assistir, de anunciar e até de se relacionar com o evento. Quatro anos depois, a Copa de 2026 trouxe outras primeiras vezes, que certamente vão criar novas dinâmicas para marcas, fãs e espectadores. Essa é a primeira Copa pós-inteligência artificial generativa. Um ponto de atenção aqui é ver uma tecnologia tão potencialmente perigosa se tornar apenas engraçada quando utilizada, por exemplo, para recriar uma cena de As Branquelas com Vini Jr. e Erling Haaland. A Copa do Mundo parece ser a sua virada definitiva - de uso indevido de imagem e fábrica de fake news a… fábrica de memes. _ Essa é a primeira Copa pós-proliferação das bets. E o momento, que parecia ideal para sua consolidação definitiva e ganho de credibilidade, teve efeito contrário. As marcas de bet se tornaram tóxicas para as transmissões que patrocinaram, atrapalhando a experiência dos espectadores e gerando antipatia a todos os envolvidos. O canal, o narrador, a marca, até os jogadores. E é além de entretenimento. 61% das apostas sugeridas pela CazéTV foram perdidas. Isso sem contar na Virgínia, influenciadora não-oficial do evento, sugerindo que seus seguidores apostassem em uma improvável vitória de Cabo Verde. Enquanto essas plataformas perdem de vista os "zeros” do quanto faturam em uma Copa do Mundo, cada aposta é dinheiro real de milhões de brasileiros, que impacta na sua renda, qualidade de vida, estrutura familiar e saúde mental. Neste momento, ainda está aberto um território para marcas que quiserem se posicionar abertamente contra as bets. De todos os lugares possíveis para assistir a uma grande partida de futebol, será que os segundos de delay contariam mais do que uma transmissão livre de gatilhos para apostar? _ Essa é a primeira Copa pós-tradução automática. Eis um novo universo de interação e entretenimento na internet: a tradução automática de posts na timeline do Twitter (X). Colocada no ar em março de 2026, bem a tempo. Basicamente, essa feature faz com que tweets escritos em qualquer idioma apareçam na sua timeline em português. Existe uma sinalização discreta da tradução, mas a experiência é fluida - você passa por aquele comentário como se ele estivesse realmente no seu contexto. E contexto é chave aqui, porque agora quem fala pode ser compreendido em toda a sua espontaneidade, sem precisar adaptar as suas palavras a quem ouve. Como naquele episódio clássico de Modern Family, em que a personagem de Sofia Vergara, uma mulher latina, se frustra com o marido americano porque não consegue transmitir toda a sua personalidade em inglês. “Você sabe o quão frustrante é ter que traduzir tudo na minha cabeça antes de falar? Você sabe o quão inteligente eu sou em espanhol?” Todo mundo que já tentou se comunicar em um outro idioma entende o que ela quer dizer. Nós somos naturalmente mais espontâneos onde temos mais fluência. Voltando ao Twitter (X), é justamente a espontaneidade e a total fluência do brasileiro em memes que agora começam a se espalhar pelo mundo - um post traduzido de cada vez. Nesta Copa do Mundo, um francês e um brasileiro puderam discutir como se estivessem na mesma mesa de bar, se entendendo plenamente. E bom… se ofendendo, também. Nessa Torre de Babel às avessas, a comunicação plena entre culturas encontrou no futebol um território comum para ser exercitada. “A minha parte favorita da Copa do Mundo tem sido acompanhar os brasileiros acabarem com os outros países, um por um, nesse aplicativo… Toda vez que eu vejo um tweet “traduzido do português” eu sei que vai ser a coisa mais sensacional, sem limites e precisa que eu já vi" Cronicamente online, extremamente criativo e ocasionalmente sem limites, o nosso senso de humor ganhou o mundo e ditou vários memes da Copa - agora globalmente. title: #299 | Nesta Copa do Mundo, olhe em volta
description: nas edições anteriores #297 | Escolher o caminho difícil #298 | Cadê a conversão? tempo de leitura: 4 minutos para entender 💡 Eu sempre vivi rodeada por futebol. A TV ligada passando o jogo aos fins de semana, o jornal esportivo local todos os dias no almoço, as idas ao estádio do Figueirense com o meu pai, e depois com meu marido. A imagem de um jogo de futebol é muito presente nas minhas lembranças, e na TV aqui em casa até hoje. Como deve ser para muita gente também. O meu nível de interesse pelo esporte em si oscilou no decorrer da vida, até chegar, hoje, em uma certa apatia. Quando tem um jogo passando numa quarta-feira à noite, eu já não faço a menor ideia de qual o torneio ou quem está em campo. Mas os anos trabalhando com marcas e observando o mundo em uma busca constante de pontos para conectar e análises para fazer, levaram o meu olhar para outro canto da televisão. Lembro bem do dia em que passei mergulhada em um conteúdo sobre o branding das bets no Brasil , e a partida de futebol à noite foi mais um “sinal”. Ignorando totalmente os lances, me desafiei a contar: quantas marcas de bet tem aqui? Nove. Isso era 2024. A transmissão de uma partida de futebol é um reflexo dos tempos em que vivemos. Porque o time em campo é protagonista, mas as marcas à sua volta contam uma outra história - sobre consumo, mídia e sociedade. O auge disso, claro, é a Copa do Mundo. _ Em 1958 , quando o Brasil ganhou o seu primeiro título e o mundo inteiro era apresentado a Pelé, acompanhar os lances era ou pelo rádio, ou por raras transmissões em preto e branco. A FIFA não vendia patrocínios globais, então as marcas presentes em placas de madeira em volta do campo eram locais, bem contextualizadas mesmo. No fundo da comemoração segundo gol do Brasil, dá pra ver a Telefunken - uma marca alemã de rádios e televisões. Corta para 1994, e o tetra foi transmitido ao vivo e a cores, com a icônica narração de Galvão Bueno. As marcas em volta do campo, por sua vez, já eram conhecidas como Coca-Cola, Gillette, McDonald's e Snickers. Mas o sinal dos tempos aqui é a presença de Fujifilm, Canon, Philips e JVC. O “capturar momentos”, seja em foto, seja em vídeo, estava se popularizando de forma irreversível. Por mais que algumas dessas marcas não estejam mais aqui contando a história… Já em 2002, a Copa do Mundo com sede na Coreia do Sul e Japão marcou a estreia de marcas asiáticas de tecnologia e carros, Toshiba e Hyundai. E o pentacampeonato foi celebrado com outra revolução como plano de fundo - a da internet. (história sendo escrita - não disse qual) Em 2014 nós recebemos o evento em casa e, bom… um baita trauma coletivo também. As placas de LED em volta do campo seguiram intercalando as marcas normalmente conforme o placar ia do zero ao sete sem qualquer piedade. Um dos maiores exemplos de “anti-marketing” de todos os tempos. A ironia, aqui, ficou por conta das marcas alemãs que foram eternizadas nos pesadelos de muita gente - Continental e Adidas. _ Muito se fala sobre o excesso de publicidade ter transformado tudo em paisagem, e de fato não dá para discordar. Uma coisa é ter dez marcas, outra é ter centenas, em diferentes formatos e canais. A Copa de 2026 é uma demonstração inegável disso. Nas últimas semanas, todos os dias teve alguma ação de marca - brindes colecionáveis (de desodorante à delivery), coleções de moda, campanhas publicitárias. Do Ronaldo ao Cafu, até o russo que virou meme em 2018 , está todo mundo virando garoto propaganda. Das transmissões online e conteúdo nas redes sociais aos produtos físicos, se depender das marcas vai ter Copa pra todo lado. (até na pia da cozinha) Mas, apesar da corrida pela atenção ser uma constante para nós, uma ocasião que acontece a cada quatro anos torna tudo um pouco mais ritualístico, mais nostálgico e mais potencialmente histórico. Porque a única certeza que a gente tem nesse mundo acelerado, é que o esporte é o mesmo, mas a próxima Copa do Mundo vai acontecer em um contexto bem diferente dessa. Que já está sendo diferente da anterior. O olhar atento para a Copa do Mundo nos leva das TVs em preto e branco até as criptomoedas. Isso torna as marcas em volta do campo parte de uma narrativa maior. Um espelho do presente - com suas tecnologias, suas questões sociais e, de uns vinte anos para cá, seus memes também. description: nas edições anteriores #296 | O futuro do futuro, pós-SXSW #297 | Escolher o caminho difícil tempo de leitura: 5 minutos para entender 💡 Enquanto profissionais de branding, espera-se que a gente passe a maior parte do tempo no topo do funil - ali nas estratégias para tornar a marca mais conhecida e reconhecida. Mas, nos últimos anos, falamos tanto de brandformance que não é inversão de prioridades questionar como as coisas estão no fundo do funil. Não dá para pensar em posicionamento ou estratégia sem entender o que está impactando o momento da conversão. Das “buscas-zero-clique” levando menos pessoas para o site às principais ferramentas de anúncios aumentando preços e dando pouca clareza dos seus dados, as estratégias que já funcionaram não são mais garantia de sucesso. E antes fosse uma conversa apenas sobre dashboards e otimizações. Mas a gente está falando de comportamento. De pessoas cada vez mais imersas nas suas bolhas, fazendo escolhas dentro de nichos com linguagem e estética próprias. Pessoas que são difíceis de segmentar com base em critérios generalistas como demografia ou geração. “O brasileiro passa mais de 9h por dia conectado” não é mais insight. E nem “precisamos estar nas redes sociais porque é lá que as pessoas estão”. Quando abre o celular, o tempo do brasileiro está espalhado por diversos aplicativos que mal aparecem em reuniões de planejamento: um joguinho de Tetris, o app do ônibus, o SofaScore ou até um app de hobby como treino, música ou cinema. E onde tem atenção, tem lembrança, consideração e conversão. _ A Voxus faz mídia programática para diversas marcas no Brasil, com a missão de potencializar conversões. E tem aprendido que isso significa ir em direções totalmente diferentes. Segundo dados da plataforma: Tem rede de academia vendendo em jogos de Tetris. Os aplicativos que mais geram conversões para uma das maiores redes de academia do país são Block Blast e SofaScore. O segundo, a cada 300 impressões gera um usuário para a marca. Parece que o público que treina também confere a tabela do Brasileirão antes de dormir… Tem farmácia convertendo em portais de notícia. O mais comum quando a gente pensa em farmácia talvez seja “aparecer onde as pessoas buscam medicamentos”. Mas os melhores canais de conversão para uma marca do segmento foram UOL, Yahoo e o mesmo Block Blast. Junto, eles somam 22% das conversões. E sneakers premium convertem em apps de ônibus. Para uma marca global de tênis, os apps que mais performaram foram, em ordem, Cittamobi (app de ônibus), Bible Offline e SofaScore. Depois vêm R7 e Yahoo. Nenhum deles canais de moda ou lifestyle . Ao invés disso, aplicativos que fazem parte da vida das pessoas de outras formas. _ Três segmentos totalmente diferentes, com perfis de clientes diferentes, têm em comum o mesmo joguinho de Tetris como canal efetivo na sua estratégia de mídia. Segundo o time Voxus , os jogos casuais “viraram um inventário de atenção que o mercado ignora porque não tem glamour de mídia. title: #297 | Escolher o caminho difícil
description: nas edições anteriores #295 | Um breve guia de rebranding - especial B2B #296 | O futuro do futuro, pós-SXSW tempo de leitura: 4 minutos para entender 💡 “Escolher o caminho difícil” foi como a Raíza Costa resumiu o seu processo criativo em um dos vídeos mais legais dos últimos tempos: “Como criar sem copiar”. Para as suas produções, escolher o caminho difícil significa buscar referências fora do digital, desenvolver uma linha criativa, trocar efeitos especiais e IA pelo trabalho feito à mão e saber lidar com as imperfeições. Porque é isso que torna o seu trabalho diferente de tudo. Os pontos que se conectam de forma inusitada no meio da água, e não em frente à tela. E as alternativas que só surgem quando o plano A dá errado. O resultado são objetos produzidos inteiramente à mão, cenas desenhadas no caderno, estúdios cheios de gente para executar tudo nos mínimos detalhes. E, claro, vídeos e campanhas que viralizam toda vez. Algo que a gente reconhece como criativo, original e inspirador só ganha forma por causa das idas e vindas do processo, e nunca apesar delas. _ Tenho certeza que o trabalho da Raíza poderia ser mais fácil em muitos sentidos. Assim como o meu e o seu, muito provavelmente. Porque o que não falta são tecnologias e soluções prometendo mais conveniência. Ou além: inserindo tanta facilidade nas nossas vidas, que de repente as coisas mais simples parecem difíceis. É mais fácil comprar uma fita 3M com frete grátis e entrega no dia seguinte. Mas 30 reais fazem bem mais diferença para a loja de bairro do que para uma gigante do ecommerce - por mais que isso exija alguns minutos de caminhada. É mais fácil fazer um pedido no restaurante depois de ter visto várias fotos dos pratos na timeline. Mas pode ser uma interação muito mais legal se deixar surpreender pela sugestão da casa. É bem mais fácil copiar e colar textos inteiros direto de uma IA. Mas escrever quando algo inspira de verdade ou quando uma ideia precisa ser organizada e deixar com que ela se desenrole é muito melhor para quem escreve, e para quem lê. Só que também é mais cansativo. Quando tudo à nossa volta nos convida para a conveniência, fazer as coisas do jeito difícil é de fato uma escolha. _ E se cada escolha é uma renúncia (já dizia o poeta) , do que estamos abrindo mão quando escolhemos, em tudo, o caminho mais fácil? É uma troca justa, por alguns minutos economizados aqui e ali? Uma ida a menos até uma loja. Uma interação a menos com um garçom. Um conteúdo a mais alimentando um algoritmo que nem finge que liga mais se algo é real ou não. Tem alguém se sentindo verdadeiramente mais produtivo, mais criativo, mais relaxado, por delegar cada vez mais de si das suas inconveniências? Ou será que do outro lado de tanta facilidade a gente não está encontrando cada vez mais nostalgia, saudosismo, retorno a tempos mais analógicos, em que as coisas demoravam um pouco mais? É curiosa essa busca recente por voltar no tempo, que leva a gente a comprar um monte de objetos - como se a solução estivesse em uma câmera menos digital, e não em uma mudança de estilo de vida. Em uma série de escolhas, conscientes e certamente inconvenientes, pelo jeito mais difícil de fazer algo - esse que a Raíza Costa conhece bem. Um jeito menos automatizado, mais demorado, mais repleto de imperfeições. title: Objects with Narratives presents collectible design that looks "found rather than fabricated"
description: Belgian gallery Objects with Narratives has curated a texture-heavy exhibition at PAD London called What Remains?, featuring pieces from Ben Storms and Paul Cocksedge . What Remains? marks the second show that Brussels platform Objects with Narratives has presented at design fair PAD London , which takes place annually in Mayfair's Berkley Square. Objects with Narratives has curated a PAD London exhibition called What Remains? The emerging Brussels gallery's exhibition brings together a series of textured pieces united by amorphous shapes and patinated surfaces. "Every piece was crafted in the present, yet many carry a sense of the past, as though found rather than fabricated," said Objects with Narratives. The show features pieces by Ben Storms and Paul Cocksedge Among the exhibitors is Belgian designer Ben Storms , who is known for his rough-hewn furniture that looks like jumbo pillows . Storms is presenting his most recent design, a cushion-like coffee table called Ex Hale, crafted from veiny red Mexican onyx decorated with mosaic veneer. To create the piece, the designer used a hydroforming technique to blow up two pieces of metal sheet that were welded together and 3D-scanned to form a cushion shape. Sofie Middernacht is showing gleaming crimson furniture After this, Storms used a CNC machine to mill the same shape from a block of stone. "Ex Hale plays with our common notions of materiality," said the gallery. "The hard stone looks soft instead, an impression that is further enhanced by the delicate surface treatment." Also on display are Jojo Corväiá's glazed vessels crafted from volcanic clay Also on display is Critical Mass, a handmade Corten steel standing shelf by British designer Paul Cocksedge . A trio of metal components were arranged to support three metal shelves, forming a piece that looks familiar to What Nelson Sees , a weathering steel installation by Cocksedge that was placed in Trafalgar Square for last year's London Design Festival. "The Critical Mass series holds an energy, something on the edge of collapse or explosion," said Objects with Narratives. Read: Armadillo furniture is clad in reused shingles to resemble "friendly monsters" Belgian designer Sofie Middernacht is showing a steel credenza, bench and duo of stools clad in gleaming crimson resin. Middernacht works with discarded industrial materials to create her furniture, which is purposefully formed like archaeological artefacts. Patchwork copper lighting by Karl Monies is included in the show Venezuelan artist Jojo Corväiá is presenting a trio of glazed vessels crafted from volcanic clay, a material central to his practice. A host of other materials feature in the show, from shaggy mohair and wool lamps by Belgian practice KRJST Studio to lighting by Danish designer Karl Monies formed from patchwork slabs of copper. What Remains? runs until 18 October "What Remains? asks what gives an object the sense that it might outlive the moment of its making: the material, the craft, or simply the possibility that some objects belong to no single time at all," Objects with Narratives concluded. Objects with Narratives was founded by Nik and Robbe Vandewyngaerde and Oskar Eryatmaz, who opened their first permanent brick-and-mortar gallery inside a historic 1920s fur atelier in Brussels in 2023. What Remains? is on until 18 October. The photography is courtesy of Objects with Narratives. PAD London 2026 takes place from 14 to 19 October 2026 at Berkeley Square, London W1J 6EN, UK. title: Frank Lloyd Wright's only planetarium restored in Florida
description: Campus architects at Florida Southern College have updated the only planetarium designed by American architect Frank Lloyd Wright as part of a decades-long restoration project at the school, which was masterplanned by Wright. The restoration included interior and exterior updates of the building, known simply as the Planetarium. The structure, which sits at one end of the Polk County Science Building, has been largely closed since 2004, when the projection system stopped working. Florida Southern College has restored and reopened Frank Lloyd Wright's only built planetarium on its West Campus. The renovation was guided by Jeff Baker, resident campus architect and a principal at MCWB Architects . Baker has worked on Wright projects at Florida Southern College (FSC) for twenty years and said the Planetarium has long been a goal. "Since the outset of these overall restoration efforts, the college was always looking for an opportunity to restore the Planetarium, knowing full well its potential to excite and inspire audiences of all ages as they get a glimpse into the heavens and the great genius of Frank Lloyd Wright," Baker told Dezeen. Work on the exterior renovations began in 2021 Work on the exterior began in 2021. The team replaced the roof, flashings, failed stucco on upper portions of the facade and replaced over 280 hand-cast "textile" tiles that line the building's perimeter. The team then moved inside starting in 2023, where "decades of interventions since Wright's death had dramatically altered the room", according to Baker. The team updated 280 tiles that line the perimeter of the Planetarium The team updated the Planetarium's technology and audio, repainting the walls from a deep blue, and paring down or removing insertions such as a computer closet built in the 1980s. It also included working with local craftsmen to restore the original Wright-designed seating made of plywood and colored vinyl upholstery, and repositioning it to its rightful orientation. Interior updates included paring down the space to its original structure and finishes "The removal of the old computer closet retrieved the space as it was designed," said Baker. "This removal allowed us to restore and reinstate all the seating in its original circular form, which we learned is a very rare survival in planetariums throughout the country." Other updates included reinstating the original paint and plaster, and restoring the floor in a "Cherokee Red" finish. The team also restored the Planetarium's original Wright-designed seating It is one of thirteen Wright buildings built between 1938 and 1958, which the university has been updating since 2007. Previous restoration work included updating the Waterdome, Wright's largest built fountain, the Esplanades, monolithic covered walkways that traverse the campus and the towering Annie Pfieffer Chapel. Technology and audio systems were also modernised and updated Baker said, like working on other buildings on campus, Wright's "elemental" architecture proved to be the most challenging aspect of the project, as there are "no 'poche' spaces to hide modern building systems". "Frank Lloyd Wright spent his life conceiving architecture as a synthesis of art and structure," he said. "At Florida Southern College, this is manifested in buildings that are elemental – the concrete floors are the ceilings for the rooms below, the concrete ceiling is also the roof above." Read: Six Frank Lloyd Wright restoration projects across the US "We believe we were able to devise methods to insert these systems in sensitive ways that meet the needs of the college yet allowed us to retrieve Wright's vision for the space." The team completed the ongoing work through grants from institutions such as the J Paul Getty Foundation, which supported the preparation of the original Campus Heritage Plan in 2007. The college has used the plan as a guide to update Wright's buildings. The space is now open to the campus and the public for tours and screenings It is the only college Wright master-planned. FSC president Ludd Spivey commissioned the architect in 1938 and, deemed a National Historic Landmark in 2012, it is the largest single-site collection of Frank Lloyd Wright architecture in the world. The Planetarium is now open to the campus and public for tours and screenings. title: Schemata Architects restores guesthouse nestled in ancient Irish rainforest
description: Japanese studio Schemata Architects has renovated a guesthouse in Dromgarriff Rainforest, Ireland , connecting two existing stone buildings with a timber- and steel-framed yoga studio. Named Linden House, the building is one of five guesthouses spread across the 39-hectare woodland in Glengarriff, which is one of Ireland's last temperate rainforests and a protected ecological area. After the site was purchased in 2022, its owners began to conserve and rewild the forest, funded partly by the transformation of its existing guesthouses into a wellness retreat. Schemata Architects has renovated a guesthouse in Dromgarriff Rainforest Schemata Architects was tasked with redesigning one of these guesthouses, connecting two stone-and-slate buildings overlooking Bantry Bay with a new yoga space shared by its 10 bedrooms. "The existing buildings consisted of two structures connected by a passageway," Schemata Architects founder Jo Nagasaka told Dezeen. "We envisioned extending this passage toward the south and transforming it into a yoga facility for the retreat centre," he added. A new yoga studio connects its two existing stone buildings The social spaces of Linden House occupy the ground floor of the longer western volume, which steps down into a large living area overlooking the bay through a fully-glazed gable end. Three of the guesthouse's ensuite bedrooms occupy the northern end of this longer volume, with a further three tucked beneath timber-framed gable ceilings on its first floor. The remaining four bedrooms occupy the smaller eastern wing, the largest of which has a double-height seating area with a matching glazed gable end facing the bay. A sawtooth roof and existing stone walls frame the studio Connecting the two wings is the yoga studio. It is framed by the exposed stone walls of the buildings on either side and sheltered by a timber- and steel-framed sawtooth roof that incorporates skylights. "The two buildings are set at an angle to one another, and by connecting them while embracing this twisted relationship we were able to create a distinctive spatial experience and form," Nagasaka explained. Read: Ómós guesthouse designed to "feel like nothing else in Ireland" "The most distinctive element is the hybrid sawtooth roof, which integrates daylighting and power generation," he added. "The north-facing surfaces bring in indirect daylight, while solar panels are installed on the south-facing surfaces to generate electricity from direct sunlight." The social spaces are held on the ground floor A desire for the new finishes to echo the guesthouse's original materials led to the studio's use of timber in the studio, the pale oak finishes in the bedrooms and living spaces, and minimalist white tiles in the bathrooms. "For the new timber elements, we chose oak, the same species of tree that is native to the surrounding forest, wherever possible," Nagasaka said. "In doing so, we sought to create a connection between the architecture and the natural resources and character of the site." The guesthouse contains 10 bedrooms Linden House marks the beginning of Schemata Architects' involvement with the site, with long-term plans including the possible reconstruction of a hotel that once stood on the site. Other projects recently completed by Schemata Architects include a store for perfume company Le Labo in Tokyo with board-marked concrete walls and an office in Fujisawa City fronted by a series of oversized corrugated metal shutters . description: Welcome to the latest edition of OBJECTS QUARTERLY, a roundup of object-related items of interest published, uh, quarterly, for supporters of The Art of Noticing. Attending to objects is a sub-theme of TAoN, and a favorite subject of mine. Revisit prior OQ issues, and other mindful materialism posts, here . Enjoy ! Via Wikipedia . By Arpingstone - Arpingstone, Public Domain, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=38786 “KIM’S GAME” Today I have another object-centric attention game borrowed from fiction — borrowed twice over, in fact. It comes from a short story callled “ Kim’s Game, ” by Sadia Shepard, published in The New Yorker earlier this year. In the story, a character recalls a childhood game that his father evidently took from Rudyard Kipling’s Kim : “My father would arrange a handful of objects on a tray—an old coin, a ribbon, a rock, a thimble, that sort of thing—and ask me to memorize them. Then he’d cover the tray with a newspaper and ask me to describe what I remembered. Sometimes, he’d take something away to see if I noticed . In the Kipling novel, the game is part of Kim’s training to be a spy.” This turns out to have become a well-known game , played (with variations) by children, the Cub Scouts , the military, and others. It actually sounds like a fun exercise — and also potentially a great assignment, particularly for a writing class. (And for the record it does sound like decent spy training, too.) If you try it, or have played it in the past, tell me about it! And as always I welcome your object-centered attention games, from fiction or real life. description: * Reminder: The Savor of the Month theme for October is WATER. Details here ; Supporters can share their findings in the thread here . Check it out! Back in August, I tried a little experiment: publishing a question from my ongoing Icebreaker series as a stand-alone post, rather than a secondary item in the main newsletter. The hope was that this would encourage readers to actually answer in the comments. And it did! So I’m doing it again. All are welcome to chime in. Noticing is about other people, too. The Icebreaker series aims to help with that. There’s a central collection spot for all the icebreakers to date, here . Today’s icebreaker comes from me. What is the most recent, or most personally important, book that you’ve read twice (or more)? I would probably stipulate no children’s books; I think that’s a different discussion. But otherwise I’d be open to just seeing where the question leads — I think it’s somehow more interesting than just asking for someone’s “favorite” book. This subject of re-reading books has popped up randomly a couple of times for me lately, and made me think about how long it’s been since I’ve done it. I guess I now worry that I just don’t have enough time to repeat a book when there are so many I haven’t read once! That said, the most recent was The Ladies’ Paradise , by Zola, which I read for a second time about 10 years ago. The book I’ve read the most times is Native Son , three times (all in my 20s, I believe). What about you? Love to hear your thoughts! Leave a comment And please send your favorite icebreaker (whether you made it up or found it elsewhere) to consumed@robwalker.net . Previously: OKAY THAT’S IT! As always, I value your feedback (suggestions, critiques, positive reinforcement, constructive insults directed at me, not at anyone else , etc.), as well as your tips or stories or personal noticing rituals, things we need a word for, and of course your icebreakers : consumed@robwalker.net. Or use the comments. —> Or just click the heart symbol. That always makes my day. Pics via SignedPG Hi all, I was thinking about saving this for the next Objects Quarterly , but it deserves its own post. Here’s the story. A few weeks ago I shared an icebreaker question suggested by valued reader Judi K: “What is something you decided not to spend money on — that you now wish you had?” Among the dozens of great answers was a little tale from SignedPG about his rather charming interest in the Big Boy restaurant chain, and his resulting collection of Big Boy items involving its amusing mascot/logo character . This sparked a bit of a sub-thread about Big Boy, but that’s another matter. For today’s purposes, here’s the key passage from SignedPG: During a road trip my partner and I went into this huge antique/vintage store, and right in the front was this Big Boy plastic figurine. It was $40, maybe the size of a Coke bottle, and I wanted it badly. The problem was that in the moment I convinced myself that my collection was stupid. I saw my reflection in the glass display, and I was just mean to myself. He still thinks about this decision, with regret: “I should’ve bought that stupid piece of plastic, but really, I just wish I was nicer to myself.” And then, a few weeks after sharing this story, a funny thing happened.
